#2618. Warriors reportedly aren't paying Kristaps Porziņģis as former All-Star combats health issues

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Golden State Warriors are withholding payments to Kristaps Porziņģis on his $20 million salary as he remains away from the team, according to ESPN. Porziņģis signed a two-year, $40 million contract with the Warriors over the summer that included a $3 million guarantee for the 2027-28 season. However, to this point, he has not been able to suit up for the Warriors as he has dealt with undisclosed health problems. Porziņģis has reportedly considered stepping away from basketball altogether, but has not publicized any decisions. Porziņģis does not currently plan to challenge the Warriors on this decision, according to The Athletic.

A spokesperson for the National Basketball Players Association declined to comment when reached by CBS Sports.

Porziņģis has been dealing with health issues since the end of his tenure with the Boston Celtics. He previously disclosed a diagnosis of POTS, or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, but that diagnosis appears to be in some dispute. Warriors coach Steve Kerr said in a radio interview earlier this year that Atlanta Hawks general manager Onsi Saleh "said it's not actually POTS," but then walked back his comments a few days later.

Porziņģis has been away from the team since late September. He met with general manager Mike Dunleavy and vice president of player health and performance Rick Celebrini in mid-October; after that meeting, the Warriors announced that he would be "around the team," but that has thus far not been the case, at least publicly.

Porziņģis released the following statement on his health in October, later adding, specifically, that he does not have HIV or AIDS.

"Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap. Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon," Porziņģis wrote. "It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it. Health is wealth. Thank you for all the support."

NBA players are typically paid regardless of health status, but teams will occasionally withhold salary if they believe the player is in breach of contract. The most notable example occurred between Ben Simmons and the Philadelphia 76ers during the 2021-22 season, when Simmons wanted to be traded. The 76ers maintained that Simmons refused to play in regular-season games and failed to show up for the start of training camp, but Simmons cited his mental health as the reason for his limited engagement with the team. Simmons was eventually traded to the Brooklyn Nets, and he and the 76ers agreed to a settlement that saw Simmons recoup a portion of the withheld salary.

The Warriors are attempting to trade Porziņģis in an effort to utilize his $20 million cap figure. While he would not have trade value as a player given his health status, he is essentially an expiring contract with only that small $3 million guarantee on the books for next season. That could potentially make him valuable to a team looking to move off of longer-term money, or the Warriors could entice another team into a trade using draft picks with Porziņģis serving only as the matching salary.

Golden State has gotten off to a surprisingly successful 5-3 start this season despite Porziņģis' absence, thanks in large part to the stellar performance of Stephen Curry and the emergence of rookie Yaxel Lendeborg as a foundational player. On paper, Porziņģis is exactly the sort of player this roster needs: a center who can shoot 3-pointers to complement Draymond Green, a poor shooting power forward. As it grows increasingly unlikely that Porziņģis will ever suit up for Golden State again, though, a trade is the only real path the Warriors have to making the best of a bad situation.

#2617. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2616. It wouldn't shock me if ... NFL Week 9: Chargers fire Mike McDaniel, another QB change in Arizona

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is about the time on the NFL calendar when teams begin taking a hard look at themselves. With the arrival of Week 9, we're halfway through the regular season, and the Nov. 10 trade deadline is on the league's doorstep.

That leaves every franchise facing the same question: What are we in 2026? Should we invest in the club we have or sell off pieces and begin building for a brighter tomorrow? The answer, of course, will vary from team to team.

We could, however, start seeing some early indications of which way these clubs are leaning in response to that question as Week 9 unfolds. In our five predictions this week, three of them center around the trade deadline and/or facing the reality that 2026 is not their year and need to make moves to better themselves for 2027 and beyond. Meanwhile, there are a couple of other less existential developments that we wouldn't be shocked to see, including a rough showing from Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels.

We'll look to carry the momentum from a strong selection last week, where we accurately pinpointed a reduced snap share from Jonathan Taylor amid trade rumors and a strong performance from T.J. Hockenson. Below, you can find five storylines and/or individual performances that we wouldn't be shocked to see happen over the course of Week 9.

The Broncos have been in the thick of trade rumors leading up to the Nov. 10 deadline as they've been a team eyed as a potential landing spot for some of the top available running backs.

When you look at their 92.6 rushing yards per game average on the season, it makes sense why they'd possibly pursue the likes of Jonathan Taylor in Indianapolis, especially with the club sitting atop the AFC West and hoping to make another deep playoff run. However, that's a 10,000 ft. view of the situation in the backfield. If you zoom in, there's a possibility that the answer to their rushing woes is already on the roster.

Rookie running back Jonah Coleman had a mini breakout performance in the win over Kansas City last week. In just his second game back from returning off injured reserve due to an ankle injury, Coleman saw a team-high 11 carries and rushed for 41 yards and a touchdown. He also caught four of his five targets for 63 yards, which included a pivotal 51-yard catch-and-run on the go-ahead touchdown drive in the fourth quarter.

That flash could just be the beginning for Coleman, who should continue to break out this week against Carolina. The Panthers are surrendering 4.8 yards per carry so far this season, which is tied for the fourth-highest in the NFL. Their 140.7 rushing yards per game allowed is third-highest in the league, so this is quite the matchup for Coleman. If he takes advantage of it, he'd silence any need for the Broncos to make a move for a back before the deadline.

The Cardinals made an in-game switch from Jacoby Brissett to Gardner Minshew last week, which helped springboard them to a win over the Cowboys. Minshew threw three touchdowns in the comeback win, which helped him be named the starter for Week 9 against Seattle. It also paved the way for the organization to trade Brissett to the Baltimore Ravens. All of those moves have seen rookie quarterback Carson Beck quietly move up the depth chart. After initially serving as the emergency third quarterback, he's now the primary backup for Arizona.

At some point, this ascension up the depth chart will continue for Beck to the point where he starts games for the Cardinals this season. After taking him atop the third round last spring, the organization has to see what it has in him before embarking on the offseason and possibly searching for another option under center. I wonder if Beck's debut could come as soon as this week during Sunday's divisional matchup with Seattle.

Minshew slicing up a poor Cowboys defense is one thing, but he'll have a much more difficult challenge against a Seattle defense allowing the fewest total yards per game (250.0) through eight contests in team history. Their 4.2 yards per play allowed is also the fourth-fewest by any NFL team through eight games in the last 20 years.

The Seahawks defense is also tied for the third-most takeaways in the NFL this season, so there's the possibility of things getting ugly for Minshew and the Cardinals offense. Does it get so ugly that Matt LaFleur makes another change in favor of Beck? I wouldn't rule it out.

One of the underrated pieces of Washington's win over the Eagles in Week 8 was just how erratic Jayden Daniels was throwing the football. On the night, Daniels registered a 17.2% off-target throw rate, which is the third-highest single-game mark in his career (including playoffs). If that persists in this matchup against the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday, Daniels' currently immaculate interception rate could shatter.

Coming into Week 9, Daniels, who has been limited to five games due to an elbow injury, has yet to throw an interception. He's just the sixth player in NFL history to have at least 240 yards of total offense per game and zero interceptions through five starts. In fact, Daniels hasn't even lost a fumble, so he has no turnovers whatsoever so far in 2026. Something tells me that changes in Week 9.

The Rams are tied for the fifth-most interceptions (7) on the season and are coming off a Week 8 win over the Chargers, where they picked off Justin Herbert twice and forced a fumble (recovered). Oftentimes, turnovers come in bunches, and if Daniels' throws continue to be all over the place, it could cost him. If the Rams, who are a 5.5-point road favorite, build a lead and force Daniels and the Commanders into a pass-heavy game script, it only adds more opportunity for the secondary to create multiple turnovers and stain his currently pristine record.

Bijan Robinson enters Week 9 as the NFL rushing leader with 780 yards on the ground thus far. However, by looking at him over the last four weeks, you wouldn't really know it. Over the past four games, Robinson's rushing totals have taken a precipitous fall, averaging 4.4 yards per carry and 71.5 rushing yards per game. Those figures are well off the otherworldly pace he was on over the first four weeks of the year.

Week 9 presents a great opportunity for Robinson to get back to something closer to the production we saw over the opening month. Entering this international matchup in Madrid, Cincinnati is allowing 122.3 rushing yards per game, which is just outside the top 10 in the NFL. When you dig a bit deeper into the numbers, however, they're even more advantageous for Robinson, with the Bengals allowing 4.8 yards per carry (tied for the fourth-highest in the league). In a surprisingly tight win over the Titans last week, Cincinnati let Tony Pollard rush for 117 yards and two touchdowns on 21 carries.

Joe Burrow has been one of the hottest quarterbacks in the NFL over the past few weeks, and one of the ways the Falcons could look to cool him off is by taking a ground-and-pound approach to this game. They have a back capable of taking over in Robinson, and this matchup is the perfect opportunity to take that approach. Expect a huge day for No. 7.

Sunday goes one of two ways for the Los Angeles Chargers. I don't think it's out of the realm of possibility that they pull out their first win in this home matchup against the Texans, especially if Houston's defense continues to struggle. However, if it continues the way it has for LA and the offense can't muster anything close to a respectable unit, I think we've reached the point where McDaniel is let go. Yes, there were cases to make this move weeks ago, particularly during the club's Week 7 bye, but Jim Harbaugh elected to stick with his offensive coordinator.

Coming out of the break, things didn't look improved whatsoever. In the Week 8 loss to the Rams, the offense continued to sputter. The unit ranks last in the NFL in points per game (14.1) and has the most total turnovers (17). They've also not scored a touchdown since the third quarter of Week 5.

This season, the Texans defense hasn't been as ferocious as it was in 2025. They've allowed 30-plus points three times this season after doing so once in 2025 and have also allowed three 300-plus-yard passers after allowing zero last year. Even if Houston looks more like their 2025 version following the bye week, the optics of struggling against a beatable defense yet again will continue to bring things to a fever pitch with McDaniel.

A loss would bring them to 0-8 on the season, and the club wouldn't play again until Nov. 16 when they are in Baltimore for a "Monday Night Football" matchup with the Ravens. That extended week could be another window for Harbaugh to make a change.

#2615. NBA Panic Meter: Why Nuggets, Heat, Suns should be worried after just two weeks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We've now seen two weeks of the 2026-27 season. Is that enough time to draw conclusions? Almost certainly not. No team has even played 10% of its schedule yet, and outlier stretches are inevitable. Case in point: last year's champion, the New York Knicks, had a mostly healthy 2-9 stretch last January that included losses to the tanking Dallas Mavericks and Sacramento Kings. Weird things can happen for a few weeks.

But the first few weeks give us our first taste of who these teams are, and inevitably several will be worse than we expected. We may not have seen enough of a sample at this point to write anyone off completely, but alarm bells are starting to ring in a few notable markets. So let's go through a few of these struggling teams and figure out just how much reason there is to panic after two weeks.

It's easy to forget this now, but New York's championship season started relatively slowly. The Knicks won their first two games, but lost their next three. Mike Brown gave a lengthy and informative monologue about some of their process issues after one of those losses, a road defeat at the hands of the Milwaukee Bucks, and the Knicks righted the ship from there. And aside from that disastrous January stretch, they were mostly great.

It's hard not to look back on that stretch now, as the Knicks limp through a slow start to their title defense. Brown has echoed many of the same criticisms he made last October, most notably the offense's tendency to stand around rather than committing to the all-out motion machine that powered the greatest playoff offense of all time last spring. Perhaps that style wasn't fully replicable for this group across 82 games. That doesn't mean it can't be summoned again in April. All four Knicks losses have come by single digits. I'm going to need more than two weeks before I start worrying about Jalen Brunson's team in clutch settings. The Knicks were the fourth-most efficient late-clock shooting team in the NBA this season. They're 28th so far this season. That's going to change.

Brunson's offseason wrist surgery is a reasonable concern. His shooting is down from everywhere, even the foul line. Maybe he'll need a midseason break to get right. Mikal Bridges is (slowly) starting to make shots again. He needs to be more aggressive, and his on-ball defense has slipped. He was never going to match the intensity he played with in the postseason given his aversion to contact, but he'll have to improve on this front. Karl-Anthony Towns needs to stop fouling, but that's hardly new. Josh Hart is missing too much in the paint, but it's too early to draw conclusions there. OG Anunoby will start making 3s because he always does.

The October Knicks look like a team that spent July, August and September celebrating. If they still look like that in December, panic becomes reasonable. For now, the concerns are relatively light. They have a proven formula, and the big concern that did exist before the season -- the backup center situation -- has thus far been a relative strength. A championship earns you quite a bit more grace than the rest of these teams deserve.

If you shouldn't write off teams after two weeks, then you certainly shouldn't do so to rookies. Still, Darryn Peterson has certainly been the worst of the much-ballyhooed top four in June's draft. He's never getting to the basket or the line, not quite prerequisites for stardom at his size given his shooting, but enormously important traits for an aspiring star guard. Defense has been an adventure as well, though that's to be expected for a rookie guard, and the early returns on his fit with Keyonte George have been clunky. The Jazz ranking 29th in offense for any stretch in which they're actively trying to win is jarring. Will Hardy had the Jazz in the top five offensively in his debut 2022-23 season before the front office broke up the team at the trade deadline.

One of the motivating factors in selecting Peterson over Rookie of the Year favorite Cameron Boozer was February's acquisition of Jaren Jackson Jr., who is currently sidelined with a torn MCL. Considering his injury history in Memphis, his long-term reliability poses real concerns, yet Utah banked most of its interior defense on him, at least in the short term, when it traded Walker Kessler to the Lakers. It's hard not to wonder about an alternate timeline in which the Jazz chose Boozer and kept Kessler instead of trading for Jackson.

If we were purely talking about the 2026-27 season, the panic meter would be higher here. We're not. The Jazz wanted to be competitive this season. There's still plenty of time for that to happen, and the eventual return of Jusuf Nurkić should help on that front for a Utah team that has gotten very little out of the center position. The real championship window, even under the most optimistic projections, was always a few years down the line. The Jazz are still young and asset-rich. There's plenty of time to right the ship. Teams with more invested in this season specifically can't say the same.

The defense is bad, but the defense is always bad. They're at the bottom of the league in 3-point volume, but they're always at the bottom of the league in 3-point volume. Aaron Gordon is no longer finding easy looks at the rim nor finishing remotely effectively, but he's spent most of the last two seasons hurt, so he might simply need time to work himself back into a groove. These were predictable concerns. Nikola Jokić was supposed to paper over them like he always does.

So far this year, he hasn't. The best player of the 2020s is suddenly human, and the Nuggets are not built to win with Jokić as anything less than divine. His own defense has been perpetually shaky, but he's always at least been an elite possession-finisher. Since becoming a full-time starter in his second season, he's never had a defensive rebounding rate below 26%. He's below 22% so far this season. He's currently tying his career-high in turnovers per game, and his assists are back to single digits for the first time since 2024.

The real issues, though, are with his scoring. Jokić's overall statistical decline after a midseason knee injury last season was well documented, but what flew under the radar at the time was the precipitous decline in his 3-point shooting following a wrist injury. This was a big driver of last season's playoff upset at the hands of the Minnesota Timberwolves. Rudy Gobert didn't have to defend him out to the 3-point line, and considering Denver's shooting deficiencies elsewhere, that allowed the Wolves to completely take away the rim. Jokić is 7-of-31 from 3 so far this season. More distressingly, his legendary intermediate finishing is slipping. After five straight years in the 95th percentile or better in terms of efficiency, his runner is down to the 86th percentile, according to Synergy Sports. His hook shot, similarly dominant, is in the 50th. His free-throw attempt rate has nearly been cut in half since last season.

There's no point in talking about the defense, the shooting, or the iffy DeMar DeRozan fit if this is the case. Either Jokić is one of the best two or three players in the world or the Nuggets are not to be taken seriously as a championship contender. Jokić has earned a lot more deference than a six-game judgment. Nobody should be surprised if he's the MVP frontrunner in a month. Those other concerns will merit closer looks if he is, because even the idealized version of this roster is pretty flawed. But there's no scenario in which these Nuggets meaningfully contend if Jokić doesn't improve. For now, that's really all that matters here.

The Suns earn the dubious distinction of becoming the first team of the 2026-27 season to have their dysfunction leaked to the press. Ironically, the thing they're reportedly upset about isn't even really the problem. Chris Haynes has reported that the Suns locker room is frustrated by the roster's lack of a point guard. But Phoenix does have a point guard; it just isn't starting him. Let's compare Phoenix's offense with Collin Gillespie on the floor to how it plays without him, using stats from Cleaning the Glass.

This isn't rocket science. The Suns assist on almost 74% of their made field goals when Gillespie plays and below 60% when he doesn't. Both Devin Booker and Miles Bridges see their true shooting improve by at least eight percentage points with Gillespie on the floor. Starting Jalen Green isn't working. Whether it's in deference to his status as a No. 2 overall pick, his contract or an unfounded belief in his value, this experiment has failed. It's time to start Gillespie and add a more traditional point guard behind him.

So the point guard issues are solvable. You know what the bigger problem is? The Suns have completely lost the high-effort identity they built last season. Let's compare where the Suns ranked last year and this year in some notable areas.

Some of this comes down to bad opponents' shooting luck. Some of it is the absence of Mark Williams, because it has forced Khaman Maluach into a role he simply is not ready for (center has been perhaps Phoenix's biggest problem area). Most of it is rotational. Green isn't exactly known for playing hard or defending. Neither is Miles Bridges. Key players from last year like Jordan Goodwin, Ryan Dunn and Rasheer Fleming are playing less. The Suns simply aren't talented enough to win at the rate they did last year if they aren't playing as hard as they did then.

The Suns don't exactly have a pivot here. They don't control any of their own first-round picks in the seven-year trade window except for a 2032 selection that is currently frozen. They're not going to be able to trade Booker for a haul and reboot this thing, either. He's 30, never gets to the rim and is a declining 3-point shooter who seemingly needs to play next to the right type of playmaking point guard. His supermax contract has albatross potential. After giving up their 2033 first-round pick for Bridges, the Suns largely locked themselves into this core for the foreseeable future. There was never championship upside here, but for a team this heavily leveraged, this level of performance is simply unacceptable.

The following clip sums up one of Miami's biggest ongoing challenges:

Look at Tim Hardway here.. and then look at davion pic.twitter.com/qPTTtlY0Oq

The Heat have a reputation, and one of its pillars is defensive tenacity. Davion Mitchell obviously has that in spades. But given the unorthodox roster-building challenges of using two big men as your primary shot creators, the Heat have had to embrace players that don't. Tim Hardaway Jr. is on this roster because the Heat so badly need shooting around Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. He is not yet making shots. He is also doing, well, this, defensively. Klay Thompson is getting hunted more mercilessly than almost any player in the NBA. The Heat have shooting. They have defense. They have alarmingly few players who offer both.

They have even fewer who can create their own shots. Antetokounmpo, Adebayo and Mitchell are the only members of the Heat who generated at least 30% of their made field goals without an assist. Toss Andrew Wiggins onto the pile, and everyone else who averages at least 10 minutes a game is assisted on 80% or more of their made shots.

Wiggins is averaging career-lows in everything. Miami's relatively egalitarian, pick-and-roll-less offense of a season ago suited him. Adjusting to the Antetokounmpo show thus far has been a struggle. Nikola Jović is veering dangerously close to dead money on their cap for the next four years. None of the core players, not Mitchell, nor Antetokounmpo, nor even Adebayo, is defending at the level expected. This was supposed to be a top-five defense. It's been in the bottom five thus far, and while some opponent shooting regression is coming, Miami's defense is designed to allow the very 3-pointers that are killing it.

Aside from simply having one of the best players in the world, it's hard to point to a distinct strength for the Heat. They're not shooting, defending or rebounding especially well. They're not winning the possession game. They're running quite a bit, but their transition offense ranks 24th in efficiency, according to Synergy Sports.

This is a team very much still finding itself, but it's one without many of the tools that made Antetokounmpo's Milwaukee teams work or the distinct advantages Miami's vaunted culture typically created for it. This roster is at least a trade or two away, but with minimal draft capital, addressing the holes here will be difficult. It might take multiple transaction cycles to get this right.

Antetokounmpo is in his 30s now and has a growing history of lower-body injuries. He might not have that many more prime seasons to waste. He's playing at a superstar level right now, and it just isn't clear how equipped Miami is to take advantage of that after giving up practically everything of value it had besides Adebayo just to get him.

#2611. NFL Week 9 upset alert: Texans allow Chargers their first win, Vikings overtake Josh Allen's Bills

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As remarkable as it sounds, we've reached the midway point of the 2026 regular season now that Week 9 is on our doorstep. The first half of the year has heard underdogs bark loudly, and there's no reason to think that'll subside as we barrel down this second leg of the season.

That's especially true this week as there are eight home underdogs on the Week 9 slate. Normally, this is a recipe for the league to flip on its head, particularly after a Week 8 schedule that was mostly chalk. Last week, we correctly identified the Raiders as a live road underdog as they came out with the outright win over the Jets, but favorites largely owned the rest of the schedule.

Water may find its level in Week 9, however, which is why we have three road favorites firmly on upset alert as we look forward to another week in the NFL.

Green Bay and New England have sort of mirrored each other to this point in the season. They both started the year 1-2 and have since surged back into playoff contention with 4-1 records over the past five weeks. Jordan Love leads the NFL in passing yards entering Week 8, while Drake Maye leads the league in total yards and touchdowns from Weeks 4-8. So, both of these teams are quite hot heading into this Week 9 matchup in Foxborough.

That said, injuries have plagued the Patriots offense, with wideout A.J. Brown missing Week 8 with a knee injury and tight end Hunter Henry leaving last week's win over Miami with a foot injury. Those are two pivotal outlets for Maye in the passing game that he may not have when he goes up against an emerging Packers defense.

Over the last five games, the Packers have given up 14.6 points per game, which ranks third in the NFL. With a potentially limited cast around Maye, Green Bay's strength could end up winning the day and the game.

Most of the attention for this game will go to the best-on-best matchup between the Bills offense and the Vikings defense. After all, Buffalo is averaging a league-best 33.3 points per game entering Week 9, while Minnesota is holding opponents to a league-low 13.3 points per game. Something will need to give there, and it could be the Vikings' blitz-heavy defense that has the advantage.

Coming into Week 9, Minnesota leads the NFL with a 69.1% blitz rate. Against the blitz this season, Allen ranks 20th among 31 qualified quarterbacks in passer rating (88.2) and is tied for the second-most interceptions (3). Of course, Allen's rushing ability can help negate Minnesota's pass rush, but his passing numbers against the blitz are noteworthy.

Meanwhile, this could be a solid spot for Minnesota's offense to find its footing. Kyler Murray hasn't been as dynamic under center as the Vikings hoped when they acquired him this offseason, and the team has largely won in spite of the offense. That said, Buffalo's defense is allowing 25.9 points per game this season, which is tied for 24th in the NFL entering Week 9. Playing in one of the better home-field environments also helps Minnesota's chances.

The Chargers have to win a game at some point, right? Right?! So far, nothing has worked for Los Angeles, as it is 0-7 this season and ranks last in the NFL in points per game (14.1) while leading the league in turnovers (17). The Chargers also haven't scored a touchdown since the third quarter of Week 5. It's been an unmitigated disaster.

While it's hard to imagine the tide turning, there's at least a glimmer of hope this week against a surprisingly shaky Texans defense. Maybe the bye week was enough for them to take a breather and get right, but what we've seen on the field so far hasn't been anything like what they were in 2025. The Texans have allowed 30-plus points three times this season after doing so once last year. They've also had three 300-yard passing games allowed, after none in 2025.

If they continue to look sluggish defensively, maybe the Texans open the door for the Chargers to catch lightning in a bottle at home.

Under Dave Canales (since 2024), the Panthers are a respectable 8-9 as a home underdog (11-6 ATS). If you cut it to the start of last season, Carolina is 6-4 as a home underdog, so this is not only a spot it is familiar with, but it's also come out on top with straight-up wins more often than one would think.

Yes, this matchup against Denver comes at a bad time for Bryce Young and the offensive line. Carolina's offensive line is banged up, which has led to Bryce Young enduring 11 sacks over the past two games. With the Broncos tied for the fourth-most sacks (23) in the NFL through Week 8, this, on paper, has the possibility of getting ugly.

That said, I wonder if the Panthers continue to find success as an overlooked team at home, especially having the rest advantage after playing last Thursday. Meanwhile, don't sleep on Denver having a bit of a letdown in Week 9 after pulling off a marquee win over the Chiefs last Sunday.

The NFL heads back out into international waters as the Bengals and Falcons square off in Madrid.

After watching both of these offenses last week, it's hard to see the Falcons keeping pace with the Bengals. That said, lost in Joe Burrow's six-touchdown performance was that Tennessee dropped 36 points against Cincinnati's defense. Cam Ward, who has had an up-and-down start to his career, threw for 304 yards and two touchdowns while rushing for 41 yards against a Bengals defense that is starting to get dinged up. The Bengals lost Cashius Howell (fractured wrist), corner DJ Turner (heel), and defensive end Cedric Johnson (ankle), all of whom suffered injuries against the Titans. Turner and Johnson could play this week, but the unit isn't 100%.

As for the Falcons, they are getting a boost defensively as top edge rusher James Pearce Jr. is back after serving his eight-game suspension to begin the year.

Cincinnati is also giving up 4.8 yards per rush this season, which is tied for the fourth-highest in the NFL. That suggests Bijan Robinson could dazzle on the international stage, especially after seeing Tony Pollard total 117 rushing yards and two rushing touchdowns against the Bengals last week. If it's a ground-controlled game for Atlanta, that could be the avenue to pulling off the win.

#2609. MLB free agency: Predicting landing spots for top players, including Jazz Chisholm Jr., Freddy Peralta, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Free agency is officially open. As of Monday, five days after the Milwaukee Brewers clinched the first World Series title in franchise history, eligible players are able to talk to and negotiate with all 30 teams with the hopes of finding their new employer. Some will get long-term deals worth more than most of us could ever dream of.

So who goes where? That's for agents and general managers to figure out. We already covered Tarik Skubal, so your CBS Sports experts are digging a bit deeper down the list for a new round of guessing games.

Mike Axisa: There are already rumblings that Morejon wants to start in 2027 and I reckon more than a few teams will be willing to give him that opportunity. The Cubs need all kinds of pitching, both starters and relievers, and can make it work even if Morejon can't hack it as a starter and needs to return to the bullpen. Regardless of role, he's an excellent pitcher, and few teams need as much pitching as the Cubs this winter. It's a perfect match.

Dayn Perry: Any team can use a lockdown reliever like Morejon, who's also young for a free agent. He's got the repertoire to be a starter conversion, too. The Yankees could use him, of course, and I expect they'll pay what it takes.

Matt Snyder: The Cubs badly need rotation help and Wrigley Field, thanks to Chicago wind patterns, is better suited for left-handed pitchers. The ownership there spends money, yes, but is relatively cheap given their market and money-making ability, which means they'll cheap out on Tarik Skubal (if they even try seriously, and my guess is they won't). So they'll need consolation prizes (yes, plural). Morejon will convert to starting and be one of them.

Mike Axisa: Rogers is underrated and he'll have an awful lot of suitors among teams that rely heavily on analytical models this offseason. He has four pitches that grade out as above average, plus he's already demonstrated the ability to get chase out of the zone and limit weak contact. It feels like he's a tweak or two away from becoming a frontline starter, or very close to one. The Mets match up well. They're data-heavy and they need a starting pitcher.

Dayn Perry: Even with some injured arms in line to return at various points in 2027, the Cubs still need rotation help, especially since they share a division with the champion Brewers. I can't see the Ricketts family, who doesn't spend nearly as much it should given the deep coffers the Cubs have, paying for Tarik Skubal. So Rogers it is, since he's arguably the second-best rotation arm on the market.

Matt Snyder: The Braves were hit with a litany of pitching injuries last season and still won the division, but there are a ton of question marks here. Spencer Strider and Spencer Schwellenbach are on that list for sure, but what about Chris Sale? He's heading toward his age-37 year and there's a club option for 2028 before he hits free agency. Grabbing Rogers here provides immediate help, depth and -- assuming it's a long-term deal -- an option to take over as the top lefty once Sale is out.

Mike Axisa: The Cubs have long been rumored as a landing spot for Peralta because of the Craig Counsell connection, though I like the other Chicago team as a fit better. The White Sox are on the rise and they badly need starting pitching. Openers and bullpen games work great in moderation. When you're doing it three or four times each turn through the rotation, it's too much. Peralta will take the ball every five days like clockwork and he's a pretty darn good pitcher too. The ChiSox need both the reliability and upside.

Dayn Perry: Yeah, I'm going with the upset here. Peralta improved significantly under the Rays' watch after the deadline deal that brought him there from the Mets, which means this tracks as a mutually beneficial relationship. With a new ballpark all but assured and a forthcoming CBA that should benefit smaller markets -- and with Stu Sternberg no longer in charge -- the Rays may be poised to actually spend a little.

Matt Snyder: We know that Jerry Dipoto doesn't like to sit still and after the Mariners came within one win of their first World Series, they were bad in 2026. They are still built to win now, especially in an awful division, but they'll reshape the team. I could see trades of starters Logan Gilbert and/or George Kirby that create the need for a rotation replacement in free agency, and Peralta would surely love pitching in that ballpark.

Mike Axisa: Ernie Clement crashed hard in the second half and has always fit better as a super utility guy who moves around rather than someone who plays one set position every day. The Blue Jays desperately need a power infusion, particularly from the left side of the plate, and Chisholm's defense and baserunning will fit in nicely as well. I wonder if any teams would show interest in Chisholm at third base or center field, two positions he's played in the past. Second base in Toronto is my best guess for now.

Dayn Perry: Detroit had pretty good luck with another outgoing Yankees second baseman (Gleyber Torres), so why not another? Jazz is coming off a down season, but he's not far removed from a 2025 campaign that was one of his best ever. A mid-term deal with opt outs aplenty makes sense here, or maybe even a high-AAV one-year pact.

Matt Snyder: There are two picks in one here, as I'll predict the Diamondbacks trade Ketel Marte and that leaves an opening to grab Chisholm for second base. It might be a one-year deal where Chisholm bets on himself to bounce back from a huge step back from his career year in 2025.

Mike Axisa: President of baseball operations Chris Young has already talked about his team needing more grit and being better at rising to the occasion offensively. That's Arozarena, who can be a flashy player but is also tough and hard-nosed, and has shown time and time again that he is unafraid of big moments. He needs to DH full-time at this point in his career and the Rangers can give him that runway. A righty power bat to complement Brandon Nimmo and Corey Seager feels imperative.

Dayn Perry: Arozarena is coming off an excellent season with Seattle, and the Phillies, still trying to make the most of their closing window, badly need an upgrade at the outfield corners. Philly hasn't been shy about investing in the on-field product, which means adding the likes of Arozarena would be fully in character.

Matt Snyder: The Phillies' window of contention remains open, even if not for long, and team president Dave Dombrowski isn't shy about adding short-term fixes to his roster. Adolis Garcia didn't work out last year, but that doesn't mean Dombrowski will be shy this time around. They still want to win a World Series with this nucleus and they need corner outfield help, among other things.

#2607. NFL Week 9 picks: Our experts face off on Jaguars at Ravens, Bengals vs. Falcons and more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's safe to say that last week lived up to the hype. The Detroit Lions defeated the previously undefeated Minnesota Vikings, the Denver Broncos used a goal-line stand to hand Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs their second consecutive loss, and the Chicago Bears upset the Seahawks in Seattle with some help from trade-deadline addition Jeffery Simmons.

This weekend in the NFL, the Cincinnati Bengals and Atlanta Falcons will battle in Madrid, Jordan Love takes the Green Bay Packers to Foxborough to play the New England Patriots and Baker Mayfield gets a shot at Caleb Williams and the red-hot Bears.

Which teams should you pick in Week 9, and which should you fade? CBS Sports writers Jordan Dajani and Jared Dubin are here to break down the biggest games of the weekend. For clarity, lines for these selections were taken on Nov. 4 from DraftKings Sportsbook. Credit to CBS Sports Research for its hard work.

Dajani (Jaguars -10): It's tough to pick this game since we are unaware of the Baltimore Ravens' quarterback situation. Will they be starting rookie third-stringer Joe Fagnano, or someone else? I believe the Jaguars will win, but any team can cover a double-digit spread at home.

Jacksonville is a remarkable 14-3 over its last 17 games and is the only NFL team leading its division by three or more games. Trevor Lawrence leads the NFL in passer rating (112.6), while the Jags lead the league in points per game differential (+12.1). Sure, you can say the Ravens will just ride Derrick Henry, but the Jaguars have what is statistically the No. 1 run defense in the NFL, and have gone 24 straight games without allowing a 75-yard rusher. …  Prediction: Jaguars 28, Ravens 13

Dubin (Jaguars -10): The Ravens simply do not have the horses to compete with the Jaguars this week. Not with their third-string quarterback (who is coming off an injury of his own), and not on a short week. Jacksonville should roll and win with relative ease.  … Prediction: Jaguars 27, Ravens 6

Dajani (Falcons +3): I may take the upset here. I'm aware the Falcons just registered one of the most embarrassing losses of the season in Tampa, but I'm willing to overlook that given how bad the weather was. I have some questions about the Bengals. Cornerback DJ Turner has a heel injury, and Cashius Howell just broke his wrist. Then, this Cincy defense allowed the lowly Tennessee Titans to put up 440 yards of total offense last week and allowed the first Titans' 300-yard passing game since the 2023 season. Tony Pollard rushed for 117 yards and two touchdowns, so what is Bijan Robinson going to do? Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are the best wide receiving duo in the league, but the Bengals may be due for their first loss in over a month. Remember, this Falcons team beat the San Francisco 49ers the last time they played a game indoors. Give me the points. …  Prediction: Falcons 27, Bengals 23

Dubin (Bengals -3): The Cincinnati offense is rolling, with Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins dunking on opposing defenses. Meanwhile, the Falcons have been struggling to run the ball as of late despite the presence of Bijan Robinson (48 carries for 200 scoreless yards in the last three weeks). The Bengals do provide an opportunity for the run game to get back on track (4.8 yards per carry allowed), but Dexter Lawrence has shut down other rushing attacks before. If the Bengals can keep Robinson in check, I'm not sure Atlanta can count on Michael Penix Jr. to go shot for shot with Burrow.  … Prediction: Bengals 27, Falcons 20

Dajani (Rams -5.5): I think the Washington Commanders are a feisty team that could cover this number, but don't forget that this is somewhat of a revenge game for Sean McVay. He spent seven seasons in Washington before the Rams made the smart decision to hire this 30-year-old kid to run their franchise. In his first season as a head coach, McVay lost to his former team. Since then, he's 2-0 vs. Washington, winning each game by at least eight points. The Rams are coming off back-to-back wins by 14+ points. They also could get Myles Garrett back on Sunday. LA is 11-2 SU and 10-3 ATS in its last 13 games vs. teams entering below .500.  …  Prediction: Rams 27, Commanders 17

Dubin (Rams -5.5): The Rams have finally climbed back to .500 with back-to-back wins over the Raiders and Chargers, and I think they can keep things rolling here by doing what they did against those two teams: running the ball. Washington has actually been pretty good against the ground game this year, but it just lost Daron Payne to a significant injury. On the other side of the ball, I don't think we can count on the Commanders' offense to produce enough points to keep up with LA's offense.  … Prediction: Rams 24, Commanders 16

Dajani (Broncos -2.5): I told you the Broncos would beat the Chiefs last week. The conversation around Bo Nix is so bizarre to me. He's not Josh Allen, obviously, but he's not worth benching either. He's not the most prolific passer in NFL history, but he's Superman when it comes to leading his team to wins in crunch time. Denver does have a great defense, which pulled off that goal-line stand vs. Kansas City, but Nix leads the NFL since 2000 with 9.1 yards per attempt when down by one score in the fourth quarter. He has 15 game-winning drives to his name, which is one shy of the most in a three-season span in NFL history. Nix hasn't even played three full seasons. It hasn't always been pretty, but Nix is pretty good in those fourth quarters.

This week, Denver travels to take on the Carolina Panthers. Bryce Young's offensive line has some serious issues, and those were evident last week against the Packers. Through Week 8, Carolina has allowed 23 sacks, which is tied for second-most in the NFL, with 11 of those sacks coming in the past two games. Plus, the Panthers' defense has allowed an incredible 42.7 points per contest in their first three home games, which eventually led to the firing of defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero last week.  …  Prediction: Broncos 24, Panthers 20

Dubin (Broncos -2.5): I'm not buying into Nix as much as Dajani is, but I am buying into Denver's defense being able to get after Bryce Young behind what is an increasingly leaky offensive line and preventing the Panthers from denting the scoreboard. If they can keep this a low-scoring game, I like them to pull out a win on the road.  … Prediction: Broncos 23, Panthers 17

Dajani (Packers +3): The Packers got some extra rest following their Thursday win over Carolina, while the New England Patriots couldn't run away from the Miami Dolphins. This Packers offense has been fun to watch — not counting the ground game,  which has registered the fewest rushing yards (485) by a team above .500 through eight games in NFL history. However, Jordan Love leads the NFL with 2,246 passing yards, while Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are the first duo to have 600 yards receiving each through eight games since Jaylen Waddle and Tyreek Hill in 2022! Drake Maye has been great, having scored at least three touchdowns over five straight games, but this Packers defense will provide quite the test. Green Bay has allowed just 14.6 points per game over its last five.   …  Prediction: Packers 27, Patriots 24

Dubin (Packers +3): I also think Green Bay's extra rest will matter here, even if only because it will give Christian Watson some extra time to heal up from the ribs injury he suffered last Thursday night. The Packers are going to need him against New England, even if he ends up drawing shadow coverage from Christian Gonzalez, as that will just open things up for Matthew Golden and Tucker Kraft. Meanwhile, Green Bay's defense has been excellent for several weeks now, and with the Patriots down multiple weapons in the passing game, I think the Packers can try to make New England one-dimensional here, limiting their chances to move the ball downfield.  … Prediction: Packers 26, Patriots 20

Dajani (Bears -6): I correctly chose Chicago to cover in Seattle last week, and I became even more confident in that pick when the Bears traded for Jeffery Simmons. The Seahawks' addition of Quenton Nelson is a great one, but I think the addition of Simmons is even better. He's the best defensive tackle in the NFL and makes life incredibly difficult for quarterbacks. In his first game for his new team, he recorded six tackles, one sack and two tackles for loss. Chicago's defense allowed just 3.0 yards per play with him on the field. The Bears allowed 13.3 yards per play with him off the field. Insane. I said last week Caleb Williams was reminding me of Josh Allen, and I think more people now agree with that assessment. He's averaged 286.7 passing yards per game with four touchdowns and zero interceptions since returning from injury.

As for the Buccaneers, it's tough for me to have takeaways from their victory in a Category 6 hurricane. We need to give Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell credit for becoming the first duo to ever rush 25 times each for 125 yards in a game against what was a top-four run defense, but Baker Mayfield is going to have to throw the ball vs. the Bears. He's thrown for just 64 yards combined in his last two games and is 1-12 in primetime since 2021, which ranks worst in the NFL. Soldier Field is going to be jumping for this Sunday night game. I'm backing the Bears.  …  Prediction: Bears 30, Buccaneers 20

Dubin (Buccaneers +6): I'm still taking Chicago to win this game, but I like Tampa to keep it close using the formula it has been rolling out over the last several weeks: running the ball effectively and keeping the opposing offense off balance with well-timed blitzes and elite run-stopping. The Bears showed last week against Seattle that they can move the ball on anyone, but that doesn't mean it will come as easily as it did on Monday night.  … Prediction: Bears 21, Buccaneers 17

Dajani (Vikings +3.5): I'm a sucker for a home dog at +3.5 in primetime — especially one making a quarterback change. We don't know this for sure, but Kyler Murray is dealing with a hamstring injury, which opens the door for Carson Wentz to start. I don't think it's a stretch to believe Wentz could open up the Vikings' passing attack. The former No. 2 overall pick came off the bench in Week 1 and threw three touchdowns in a 39-22 win over the Packers. Then, in Week 2, Wentz escaped Chicago victorious, 9-3, in a monsoon. Justin Jefferson's best game of the season came with Wentz in Week 1, as he caught eight passes for 92 yards and two touchdowns. All of those numbers were season highs for him. Murray averages 170.3 passing yards per game, which ranks 30th among 31 qualifying passers. We know the Buffalo Bills boast a high-flying offense, but this Vikings defense is still the best in the NFL. They lead the NFL in points per game (13.3), passing defense (154.9 yards allowed per game), red zone touchdown percentage (25%) and sacks per game (3.6). Give me the points with Minnesota if Wentz starts. …  Prediction: Bills 24, Vikings 23

Dubin (Bills -3.5): You can't ask me to buy into this Minnesota offense right now — not even against Buffalo's leaky defense. We just saw the Vikings put up a relatively limp offensive performance against the Lions. And if there's a team out there that can run the ball on Minnesota the way the Lions did, it might be the Bills with Josh Allen and James Cook. I think Buffalo can win a low-ish scoring game here by doing just that.  … Prediction: Bills 20, Vikings 14

#2606. How busy will the MLB offseason be before likely lockout? Insiders weigh in on November's urgency, uncertainty

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Hot stove season is underway in Major League Baseball. And with a lockout looming when the current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1, the next four weeks will likely be the only time that teams have to sign free agents, make trades and reshape their rosters before transactions come to a halt.

Want some context into just how much of a mad dash this could become? One brief exchange with a head of baseball operations offered a glimpse. When asked what his club anticipated in the coming weeks, the executive offered only this: "I'm going to stiff arm you on this one," the exec said. "Because I'm time constrained right now. A lot going on with staff and player conversations."

Urgency will play a role this November. Naturally, teams don't want to be left behind. And the way modern baseball conducts business could be challenged.

Over the last five years, the early stages of MLB's offseason have been largely anticlimactic. Front offices, many of which rely on similar analytical models, have increasingly approached the market with caution, contributing to a process that can drag well into the winter.

Even the Winter Meetings, traditionally a gathering place in early December for blockbuster trades and significant free-agent signings, have increasingly become more of a launching pad for offseason conversations than a destination for completed deals.

So, what does this peculiar November have in store? Yes, there will be moves. But according to one high-ranking league executive, don't expect the approaches that have defined the modern offseason to change entirely. The urgency might be different, but the process of gathering information, evaluating talent and understanding the market remains largely the same.

"You can't get caught flat-footed, so we're going through the same motions of lining up who we like, identifying different ways to meet our needs, calling agents and letting them know we have interest," the executive said. "Next week at GM meetings will be helpful to learn more. That's usually when we indicate we want to zoom with a player and we'll see how agents/players react to that."

Trades, certainly, could take precedence over free-agent signings, given the circumstances and the talent available. This year's free-agent class is notably weak, particularly when it comes to starting pitching. The trade market, meanwhile, could offer alternatives that free agency simply doesn't.

One left-handed starter from the Los Angeles Angels, who isn't set to become a free agent until 2029, figures to be particularly coveted.

"A bunch of teams need pitching based on our initial sweepstakes," the executive continued. "So I think names like Reid Detmers will be in high demand. If you're a team in on him, it might be worth overpaying to jump the line. After [Tarik] Skubal, none of the starting pitching free agent names are that exciting."

No team wants to get left behind. But with the uncertainty surrounding 2027 and little indication of what next year might look like, teams don't want to overreact, either. The temptation to move quickly must be weighed against the consequences of making the wrong move.

Reacting to an opponent's moves, as that same executive suggested, can prove costly. Particularly in a market where the pressure to act could drive up the price of acquiring talent.

More importantly, all of this remains a moving target. The uncertainty surrounding the next season complicates even the most straightforward roster decisions. Rentals, as one front-office official put it, aren't particularly attractive given the circumstances. In the (still seemingly unlikely) event that there's no baseball in 2027, trading away prospects or valuable big-league talent for a player with only one year of control becomes a considerable gamble. A team could surrender valuable assets without ever getting the opportunity to benefit from the acquisition.

Years of contractual control carry even greater value now. Teams recognize that, which could ultimately stall trades. The very players who might offer the most security in an uncertain market could also become the most difficult to acquire.

"We're really operating under uncertainty now," one front-office person said.

Now, that isn't to suggest free-agent deals won't get done. In fact, one agent said he wouldn't be surprised to see a flurry of mid-tier players reach agreements ahead of the Dec. 1 CBA expiration, pointing to the activity leading up to the 2021–22 lockout as evidence of how an approaching deadline can accelerate an otherwise slow-moving market.

"Last time there was going to be a lockout it was extremely active for Kevin Gausman and Marcus Stroman, who were free agents entering 2022," the agent said.

Gausman signed a five-year, $110 million deal with the Toronto Blue Jays, while Stroman inked a three-year, $71 million contract with the Chicago Cubs. Corey Seager and Marcus Semien, meanwhile, agreed to huge deals with the Texas Rangers. A total of $1.7 billion in free-agent contracts were agreed to prior to the lockout.

This year, Sonny Gray, Tyler Mahle, and Gausman, again, certainly fit that second-tier group.

"Nothing motivates clubs more than a deadline, so I'd be shocked if there wasn't a flurry of deals prior to the deadline," the agent said.

Whether through trades or free agency, the expectation remains that deals will get done in the next four weeks. It will be a fascinating November.

#2603. Micah Parsons details why knee recovery has taken so long, refuses to set timeline for Packers return

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Green Bay Packers star Micah Parsons has been out since tearing his ACL during the Packers' Week 15 loss to the Denver Broncos last season. But there is some light at the end of the tunnel.

Parsons had his 21-day practice window open on Wednesday, so he spoke with local media for the first time about his injury and recovery process. However, there's still no set timeline on when he should return to the field. Even if there was, he likely wouldn't let us know.

"I just want it to be a surprise," Parsons said during his media availability regarding the timeline.  "I just want it to be a fulfilling moment for myself, the staff — just to enjoy that day and not put too much pressure on that day. My family [has] even been asking me, 'You going to play? Should we buy flights to come out there?'

"But I'm not going to pinpoint a day to disappoint anyone or give people expectations that I can't meet."

Parsons noted that in addition to having surgery on the torn ACL, he had a full repair of the medial and lateral menisci in his knee. He was therefore non-weight-bearing for two months, which is why his recovery timeline has been longer than some other players who have suffered torn ACLs in recent years.

Parsons said he had to undergo in-depth conditioning to get his body back into shape, just to get to the point he is right now. But there's still a long process ahead. He doesn't expect to be his full self when he does get back into game action.

"My conditioning right now is probably the worst it's been in my career," Parsons said. "And that's just the reality of it. Am I going to go out there and play 50, 60 snaps how I was doing before? Absolutely not. It's just not realistic. My body is not there yet...So I'm not going to be the All-Pro Micah, the person I once was, this year. Probably not until later, after I go through my phases and things like that, but I think what people will see is they'll see this guy is ready to play football. He's going to play hard, and he's going to boost this defense that's already doing a great job."

"I think those types of things you won't question, and I think you'll see flashes of All-Pro Micah when I do the pass rush, and there will be times where it's like, 'Dang, what was Micah doing?' And there's going to be times I question myself too...Because the reality is I just came back from an 11-month injury."

Even though Parsons has already been out for nearly a full year and will still take some more time to return to the field for actual games, he feels like he took the right course in his rehab process. He felt "the patience was absolutely worth it" and hopes to make a full run with the team well into December and into the playoffs.

Parsons is returning to a Packers team that has turned its season around over the last few weeks. Green Bay fell to 1-2 with an embarrassing "Thursday Night Football" loss to the Atlanta Falcons in late September but has since gone 4-1, with the lone loss coming by three points against the division rival Detroit Lions. As they head into the stretch run of the season, the Packers are in position to make a playoff push. And Parsons feels as though he is getting ready to return at the perfect moment.

"I came back for the greatest time of football," he said. "And that's November football and December football. Let the show begin."

#2602. Brewers' Pat Murphy apologized to Yankees' Brian Cashman over viral comment about Jake Bauers free agency

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the aftermath of the World Series championship, Brewers manager Pat Murphy was caught on a hot mic talking to first baseman and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, who heads into free agency this winter off a career year.

Murphy's message? "You're gonna be a rich f---er, but just remember when you were on that horseshit Yankees team and you guys were all playing for yourself, just remember, say, 'this is the way we used to do it.'"

The comment, predictably, drew backlash from those who assumed Murphy was taking a shot at the Yankees. Bauers was on the 2023 Yankees, when they went 82-80 and missed the playoffs.

"I called Brian Cashman right away when I heard it got out," Murphy said on the New York Post's "The Show with Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman released on Tuesday. "I picked up a phone and called Brian right away, and had a good conversation. And the best I could try to explain that I wasn't talking about the 2026 Yankees.

"After every celebration, I'd shake his hand. I'd say, 'You rich so-and-so, you're going to leave us,' " Murphy explained. "We're not going to be able to pay you. You're going to leave us and you're going to forget all about how we did things. … I would just give him this rhetoric every time.

"I was just referring to the teams that have a lot of high-paid, long-contract players," Murphy said. "That sometimes it's harder to get all those guys together to play together. And I used the Yankees because I knew Jake was with them before. … I regret saying it, but that was Jake and I's humor behind the scenes and I got caught."

First off, dudes talking to dudes when they don't realize anyone else is listening lends itself to a lot of comments they don't necessarily mean or, perhaps more importantly, don't include the context of a longstanding relationship between a manager and his player. There isn't anything really out of line here in terms of the Yankees shot. Any Yankees fan would tell you they agree with Murphy's assessment of that team.

Where I do believe there's a problem is the insinuation that a player getting a huge payday means that he'll just start playing only for himself instead of doing things as a team. The Dodgers' high individual salaries certainly didn't stop them from winning two straight World Series titles.

Further, Bauers made $2.7 million last season, double his previous high. MLB players have a finite shelf life and need the money they make to stretch, if they're lucky, for generations. He's set to make exponentially more in free agency in his one big payday to hopefully set up his family for decades. Some might think it insensitive of Murphy to mock that a player might need to look out for himself and his family.

Then again, take note of Murphy's quote when he says that's just their sense of humor. We don't know their personal relationship because it is just that: personal. Unless Bauers signs elsewhere and comes out guns blazing against Murphy, this whole thing is probably just much ado about nothing. It would be pretty shocking if Cashman took particular offense, either.
